reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Characterised by unilateral absence of the sternocostal head of the pectoralis major muscle, giving a flat or asymmetric anterior chest wall
Ipsilateral hand hypoplasia is typical, classically with shortened fingers and cutaneous syndactyly (symbrachydactyly)
The right side is affected more often than the left, and the condition is almost always unilateral
Associated findings include absence of the pectoralis minor, breast and nipple hypoplasia or absence, and rib deficiencies
It overlaps with Moebius syndrome, and the two may coexist, supporting a shared vascular disruption mechanism
In women, breast underdevelopment may be the presenting feature at puberty
Most cases are sporadic with normal intellect, and the primary concerns are functional hand use and chest wall protection
reference.pathophysiology: Poland syndrome is thought to arise from a vascular disruption sequence, most commonly attributed to reduced blood flow through the subclavian artery and its branches during the sixth week of gestation. Interruption or hypoplasia of this vessel is proposed to compromise the developing chest wall and limb bud on the affected side, producing the absent pectoral muscle, chest wall and breast deficiency, and hand malformation. The degree and precise territory of the vascular compromise determine the pattern and severity of the anomalies, explaining the frequent unilaterality and the overlap with Moebius syndrome when the vertebral or brainstem circulation is also involved. Cases are overwhelmingly sporadic.
additionalDifferentials: Sprengel deformity with chest wall involvement
Amniotic band sequence affecting the limb
Congenital chest wall deformities such as pectus anomalies
additionalInvestigations: Chest wall and thoracic imaging to define muscle, rib, and sternal anomalies
Hand radiographs to characterise skeletal hypoplasia and syndactyly
Echocardiography where cardiac or great vessel anomalies are suspected
Assessment for dextrocardia or dextroposition in left-sided cases
Renal ultrasound if additional anomalies suggest a broader disruption
Occupational therapy assessment of hand function
redFlags: Significant rib deficiency leaving thoracic viscera inadequately protected
Paradoxical chest wall movement or respiratory compromise from extensive rib defects
Coexisting cardiac or great vessel anomaly
Features suggesting associated Moebius syndrome with feeding or airway risk
Marked functional hand impairment requiring early rehabilitation
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good with normal life expectancy and cognition; management focuses on hand function, chest wall reconstruction where protection or appearance is a concern, and breast reconstruction in affected women.
pitfalls: Regarding it as a purely cosmetic chest deformity and missing functional hand impairment
Overlooking rib deficiency that compromises thoracic protection or respiration
Failing to assess for coexisting Moebius syndrome
Not screening for cardiac anomalies, particularly with left-sided involvement
Neglecting the psychosocial impact, especially breast asymmetry in adolescence
